name: Reverb, delay, shimmer and freeze: creating depth and space
goal: Place sounds in space with sends: choose reverb type, pre-delay and low-cut, tempo-synced and ping-pong delays, distorted/band-limited delay throws, shimmer (+12 pitch in feedback), reverb freeze/reverse swells and fully-wet extreme reverb pads.

theory: Wet/dry ratio and pre-delay set perceived distance; early reflections give size; high-damping and low-cut on returns keep lows clean. Feedback < 1 decays; ~0.99 sustains (self-sustaining pad); pitch shift in the loop climbs octaves (shimmer).
prerequisites: A DAW with buses and automation
A bit crusher or distortion, EQ, compressor with sidechain, and a filter
A stereo delay with independent left/right times and feedback up to 99%
Algorithmic reverb with freeze and overdub/'add' toggle (Web Audio: feedback delay network with feedback→1 and an input-gate for overdub, implementation note)
An impulse source: short noise burst or fast high-to-low sine sweep
Bus/group routing and an audio track that can record a bus
DAW (or offline renderer) with audio reverse, bounce/export, normalize and clip fades

DAW or Web Audio graph with reverb, stereo width/imager utility, panner, ping-pong delay and filters; in Web Audio: ConvolverNode → mono sum (ChannelMerger/Splitter or a mid-only gain) → StereoPannerNode → ping-pong delay pair (implementation note)
DAW sends/returns; reverb with hall/chamber/room/plate/spring (or IR) modes; EQ after reverb on the return
Delay or pitch-shifter with feedback; long lush reverb/convolution; EQ on wet path
Delay with feedback and an in-loop filter (or DelayNode + BiquadFilter in a feedback loop / AudioWorklet)

outputs.name: result
outputs.description: Rendered part or recipe following the workflow

constraints: Portable recipe; not affiliated with any vendor; do not copy factory presets or sample packs.
Numbers in variants come from the source video transcripts; workflow steps are the consolidated mainstream practice.
Bring drums in early and avoid pitch wobble unless asked (user preferences from daily tests).

steps.action: Use sends/returns, not inserts, for shared space; one short room (0.5-1 s) and one long hall/plate (2-5 s).
Set pre-delay 10-40 ms to keep the dry attack clear; low-cut return 150-300 Hz, high-cut 6-10 kHz for darker depth.
Delay: tempo-sync (1/4, dotted 1/8, 1/8T), feedback 30-50%, ping-pong for width; band-limit (HP 300 / LP 4 kHz) and optionally saturate the return for 'throws'.
steps.expect: Rhythmic echoes that do not clutter

steps.action: Narrow a reverb to mono before a ping-pong delay to create focused 'pockets' instead of wash.
Shimmer: pitch-shift +12 st inside the reverb/delay feedback, mix 10-30%; self-sustaining pad: few notes into a ~99% feedback asymmetric stereo delay (e.g. 1 s L / 150 ms R).
Freeze/print: freeze a reverb tail or print it, reverse it for swells into downbeats, or loop it seamlessly as an atmos layer.
Extreme pad: send percussive sources (piano, vibes, glock) 100% wet into 20-40 s chained reverbs; bitcrush or brighten before the reverb; EQ the bus and sidechain it lightly.
Duck reverb returns to the dry source or kick if the mix gets washy.
Hear the theory: run `/home/box/audio-tools/bin/python sample-lab/theory/reverb_delay_space.py` from the repo root and compare the sections; reuse its functions as a starting point for renders.
steps.expect: WAV in sample-lab/theory/out/ demonstrating the principle

verification: Render a short test and A/B against a reference at matched loudness
Run the generator and confirm it writes a WAV without error
Check mono compatibility and that no element masks the kick/bass

variants.name: Distorted-delay return: drive → ping-pong delay on a 100%-wet send, both band-limited to high mids, return pre-attenuated, played by riding the send
variants.goal: Add crunchy, wide echo throws to a lead/pluck without mud or volume spikes: on a send/return insert drive then ping-pong delay, band-limit both to the high mids so lows aren't delayed, feedback ~56%, both 100% wet; dial drive/tone at maximum send, then pull the return down ~−6 dB as a safety ceiling, and perform/draw send-level automation so only chosen notes throw distorted echoes — the delta vs our ping-pong delay skill is drive-before-delay on a return and send-throw performance.
steps: Create a spare return. Insert overdrive then delay (ping-pong).
Set the overdrive's pre-filter to the high mids only, and do the same on the delay's filter so only that band is delayed.
Delay: ping-pong for width, feedback ~56%; both devices 100% wet so only effect signal returns.
Turn the send to maximum and dial drive and tone to the desired timbre.
Pull the return fader down (~−6 dB start) so maxed sends never produce super-loud output.
Perform: jam the send knob live to feel where echoes should happen, then tidy or draw send automation per note (some full, some partial).
Check in context with the full track and adjust.

variants.name: Turn bright percussive or decaying instruments (electric piano, vibraphone, piano, glockenspiel) into an evolving ambient pad by running each through 100% wet reverbs of about 20-40 s (chaining two reverbs for longer tails), bit-crushing the piano before the reverb to sustain and add harmonics, taming harsh highs with EQ, then busing the layers with a low cut, compression, sidechain and a filter that reveals the pad
variants.goal: Make an ambient pad from stock instruments rather than a synth. Pick sources with rich, bright harmonics (distorted electric piano, vibraphone, piano, glockenspiel) and play the same chords stacked across several octaves, panning some layers slightly left and right. Put each through a reverb set to fully wet with no dry signal and a very long decay (about 33 s, 22 s, 40 s in the video); daisy-chain two algorithmic reverbs to get even longer tails and lower the level. The reverb smears the transients away and effectively adds a long attack. For extra brightness and sustain, bit-crush (distort) the piano before its reverb, then EQ down the harsh upper-mid/top it added. Roll off some highs on very bright sources like glockenspiel before the reverb. Because the layers use different reverb lengths they create multiple attack phases, so the sound evolves. Bus all layers; EQ out the large low-frequency/sub-20 Hz build-up from the long reverbs, add compression, sidechain compression and a low-pass filter that you automate open to introduce the pad.
steps: Program a couple of chords stacked across several octaves; load bright sources (distorted electric piano, vibraphone, piano, glockenspiel) on separate tracks, panning a few slightly left or right.
On the electric piano, insert a reverb at 100% wet / 0% dry with about 33 s decay.
On the vibraphone, daisy-chain two algorithmic reverbs (fully wet) for an even longer tail; turn the track down.
On the piano, insert bit crusher → EQ → reverb (fully wet, about 22 s); crush fairly hard to sustain and add harmonics, then cut the harsh upper-mid/top with EQ.
On the glockenspiel, roll off some of the top with EQ before a fully wet reverb of about 40 s (chained reverbs).
Listen to all layers together: different decays give multiple attack phases that morph over time.
Route all layers to a bus: EQ out the low/sub build-up, add compression and sidechain compression, and a low-pass filter.
Automate the bus filter open to introduce the pad in the arrangement.

variants.name: Mono (narrowed) reverb as a mixing and sound-design tool: narrow each 100%-wet reverb into a placeable 'pocket', pan pockets to separate parts, put a stereo ping-pong delay after the width stage so the pocket travels left-right, use the wet/dry mix as a distance control, filter the reverb tail post-reverb with an LFO-moved bandpass, and split dry left / mono reverb right for pseudo-stereo
variants.goal: Clean up a crowded ambient or electronic mix and get new textures by making reverbs mono or narrow instead of wide. For each sound, decide what stays stereo (e.g. a wide atmos bed with high-end detail) and what becomes a pocket: narrow the reverb width (it does not have to be fully mono; side-reducing imagers sound better than fold-to-mono), then pan the pocket to its own spot and turn it down, since a centred or narrow reverb is more audible and needs less level. Put a ping-pong delay after the width utility (low feedback, lowpass in the feedback path) so the mono pocket moves left and right without washing the whole field. Treat the wet/dry mix as a distance knob: fully wet is far, fully dry is close, which is more obvious with mono reverb. Filter after the reverb with a bandpass moved back and forth (manually or by LFO), with the filter mix keeping some high end, to shape the tail as its own sound. For pseudo-stereo, put a mono reverb on a send, pan the dry sound fully left and the reverb fully right, then bus both through a driven resonant filter. A fully wet mono reverb on an atmos track, sidechained, becomes a wall of sound that sits behind the lead.
steps: Solo through the parts and decide which stays stereo (e.g. an atmos bed with high-end detail through a moving notch filter into a 100% wet reverb) and which become mono/narrow pockets.
For a pocket track, set its reverb 100% wet (on the insert) and narrow its width with a side-reducing imager or width utility, partly or fully.
Pan each pocket to its own spot (e.g. short step pocket right, layered second step slightly wider and left, main part centre) and turn levels down: narrow reverbs are more audible, so they need less.
Put the ping-pong delay after the width stage, with low feedback and a lowpass on the feedback, so the mono pocket is carried left and right.
Use the reverb mix as a distance control: fully wet = far behind, fully dry = right in front. Shave highs for extra depth.
Place a bandpass filter after the reverb and move it back and forth by hand or with an LFO; use the filter's mix to keep some high end. Post-reverb filtering shapes the tail as its own sound.

Pseudo-stereo: send the sound to a mono reverb return, pan the dry sound hard left and the reverb hard right, then route both to a bus with a driven, resonant filter (cut lows, shorten the reverb, add movement).
For a background wall: put a fully wet mono reverb on the atmos track and sidechain it to the lead or kick so it ducks out of the way.

variants.name: Reverb-freeze atmosphere print: freeze a 100%-wet reverb of a synth phrase, record it to audio, loop it seamlessly with overlapping tail, bus and process as an atmos layer
variants.goal: Create a background atmosphere layer from any melodic synth part: send it to a 100%-wet, low-cut, high-diffusion/large-size/long-decay reverb with a freeze/hold function, engage freeze while the phrase plays, record the frozen output via a group bus onto a new audio track, then EQ it, add sidechain-style volume ducking and a second ~5–6 s reverb so the loop point is masked, duplicate and overlap the clips with a short end fade for a click-free endless loop, and group the layers into an atmos bus — optionally printing separate closed-filter and open-filter freezes to follow the arrangement.
steps: Insert a freeze-capable reverb on (or as a send for) the synth phrase: cut the lows, mix 100% wet, raise diffusion, size and decay.
Play the phrase and engage freeze at the musically richest moment; the reverb holds indefinitely even when playback stops. Release/turn down to end.

Route the synth (with the freezing reverb) to a dedicated group bus, create an audio track whose input is that bus, and record a few bars (~4) of the frozen output. Then remove the temporary reverb and restore the synth's original output routing.
On the printed track: EQ low end out and tame highs; add a sidechain-style volume shaper so it pumps with the groove.
Add a second reverb on the print (low cut, ~5–6 s decay, larger size, modulation off) so the restart of the loop isn't heard as a jump.
Make the clip loop seamlessly: add a small fade at the end, duplicate it onto a second track, and overlap clips so each new clip starts while the previous tail fades.
Group both print tracks into an 'atmos' bus; process together (another large reverb with lows cut ~600–700 Hz and reduced feedback/mix, gentle top-end saturation/exciter).
If the source filter opens later in the arrangement, print a second freeze with the filter open and use closed/open layers per section.

variants.name: Reverb for pads: pick type by texture, then set up 100%-wet EQ'd send returns
variants.goal: Choose and route cinematic pad/synth reverb: decide if reverb is needed; pick type by texture not just length (hall lush 2–3s+ with mud risk, chamber thickening with less space, room/ambience intimate ~0.3–1s, plate bright attack→darker decay, spring metallic/boingy); keep 2–3 go-to returns (room ~1s, long plate ~6s, bright spring ~4s) at 100% wet on sends; high-pass returns ~200 Hz+; use pre-delay for clarity, layer short ambience under longer hall/plate, prefer shorter spaces in busy mixes, and pull send back on longer decays.
steps: Decide intentionally whether the source needs reverb (do not add by default). Match genre references.

Recall controls: pre-delay separates dry from reverb onset (clarity); early reflections cue size/material; tail/late reflections = sustain; decay = fade. Think texture/tonality more than length alone.
Hall: large auditorium character, often ~2–3s+ (longer for cinematic/atmosphere); lush/deep, thickens and pushes source back—high mud risk. Natural for piano/strings/orchestra.

Chamber: studio reflective-room character—lush thickening with less mix real-estate than hall; very versatile (pads, strings, vocals). Room/ambience: smaller/intimate; ambiences often ~0.3–1s, ER-heavy—liveliness without takeover.
Plate: mechanical metal-plate density; bright quick attack then darker decay—great sustain/sheen. Spring: metallic/boingy modulation in decay—character FX more than lush pad default.
Build 2–3 saved returns: (1) room ~1s+ decay for basic space; (2) long ambient plate (transcript example ~6.2s); (3) spring or other bright flavor (~4s). Save in template.
Use sends: set reverb mix to 100% wet on the return. Control amount only via send level so dry stays constant and wet can be EQ'd independently.
EQ the reverb return after the algo: high-pass everything below ~200 Hz (or higher) so reverb does not invent mud. Optional cuts for metallic harshness (e.g. spring).

Practice: pick type in solo for texture, set level in full mix. Layer short ambience under longer hall/plate. Busy mixes → shorter rooms/plates; sparse/ballad → longer halls/plates. Optional high-cut on reverb darkens and pushes wet further back.
Add too much send, then back off to a musical amount. Longer decays usually need less send; shorter rooms can take more. Share one long plate across lead vs backgrounds with different send depths.

variants.name: Manual reverse-reverb swell: reverse, print 100%-wet reverb, re-reverse, trim and fade into the onset
variants.goal: Make a reverse-reverb swell by hand (no dedicated plugin) that leads into a vocal, chord or hit with its own timbre: duplicate and reverse the source, print a large 100%-wet reverb of the reversed audio, keep only the part that leads into the first word/hit, reverse it back so it swells forward, normalize, align and fade it into the dry onset, and optionally give the swell its own late-automated reverb tail.
steps: Duplicate the source audio onto a second track.
Reverse the duplicate (audio process -> reverse).
Insert a large reverb (large live-stage/hall size) on that track with mix at 100% so you hear only the wet signal.
Bounce/export the soloed wet signal to a new audio file (mono in the source example).
Keep only the part that matters - the portion that leads into the first word/hit - and delete the rest and the temporary track.
Reverse the printed clip back so the reverb now swells forward into the onset, and normalize it.
Move it to just before the dry source and add short fade-in/fade-out at the clip edges to remove clicks.
Optional: put another reverb (~50% mix) on the swell channel so it has a softer tail, and automate that reverb to come in only at the last split second so the whole tail does not wash out.
Reuse on other sources: kick, cymbal crash into a breakdown, white-noise rise, pads/chords.

variants.name: Turn a few played notes into a self-sustaining shimmering pad by feeding them once into a clean stereo delay at 99% feedback with very different left/right times (about 1 s and 150 ms), so the melody dissolves into a continuous texture for the rest of the track
variants.goal: Feedback-delay pad generator. Play a short phrase of three or four notes once into a neutral (uncoloured) stereo delay; nothing else is fed in for the rest of the track. Set feedback to the maximum safe value (99%) and set the delay times far apart: about 1 s on the left and about 150 ms on the right. The repeats keep cycling through the whole track; the original melody vanishes and is replaced by a shimmering secondary texture. Optional: use a tape-style delay instead for pitch warble, which strengthens the shimmer. Use the plain feedback control rather than cross-feed, which grows the signal quickly.
steps: Write a 3-4 note phrase and route it to a stereo delay set 100% wet on that channel (or on a send).
Set left delay about 1 s and right delay about 150 ms; set feedback to 99% on both sides; leave cross-feed at zero.
Play the phrase once and let it run; do not feed more notes in.
Optional: swap to a tape-style delay with light wow/flutter to exaggerate shimmer.
Add a limiter or level automation after the delay and check the level over the full track length.

variants.name: Shimmer reverb: +12st pitch-shift into lush space
variants.goal: Build a portable shimmer (Eno-style) send: pitch-shift the wet path by +12 semitones into a long lush reverb/convolution, optionally feedback the shifted delay for endless bloom, high-/low-cut the delay echoes before the reverb, and EQ the wet shimmer before dry blend.
steps: Route a send: place a delay/pitch stage before the long reverb. Set pitch shift to +12 semitones so the shifted copy washes into the lush space.
Use a long lush reverb (or convolution with high lush/length) so the shifted signal sustains as a cloud.
For endless blossom: enable feedback on the delay/pitch path so each loop shifts again. Short delay times → rapid expansions; longer times → slower bloom intervals.
Tone-shape the delay echoes before reverb: cut lows so low end does not stack; shave brittle highs so the convolution/reverb is not harsh.
EQ the overall shimmer wet (e.g. high-pass low band; gentle brightness if needed) before blending with dry via mix/send level. Optionally explore delay after reverb or ducking wet from dry later.

variants.name: One-knob reverb → drone instrument: macro range 0–99 = wet/dry, 100–110 = muted dead zone, 110–127 = freeze + overdub drone with LFO speed, plus LFO-modulated EQ/width, unsynced auto-filter, limiter and randomizable algorithm
variants.goal: Wrap an algorithmic reverb in a macro rack that doubles as an ambient drone generator: one 'drone' macro maps wet/dry over its lower range, a 100–110 dead zone that mutes the rack (utility gain/off) to avoid the loud boom when leaving freeze, and from 110 up engages freeze-with-overdub so new notes add into the held reverb while the same macro sets a jittered, shaped LFO from fastest (at 110) to ~0.1 Hz (at the top); that LFO modulates mid-EQ frequency (+30), mid gain (−25), low edge (+15), high edge (−20) and stereo width (+15); a parallel-moving auto filter (~1.5 kHz, 10% res, ~5% drive, its own time-mode LFO at 10%) stays out of sync; a limiter guards overdub build-up; other reverb parameters (algorithm, decay, size, per-algorithm params) are randomizable, EQ/pre-delay/drone excluded, and good results saved as variations.
steps: Build a rack: algorithmic reverb (convolution off) → LFO device → auto filter → limiter → utility (gain). Expose 16 macros: algorithm, decay, size, params 1–5 (map each algorithm's own 5 controls to the same macros), low/mid/high EQ, mid gain, vintage, width, pre-delay, drone.
Reverb EQ: band 1 and band 4 as steep (48 dB/oct) edge filters mapped to 'low EQ' and 'high EQ'; bands 2+3 frequencies to 'mid EQ', their gains mapped inversely to 'mid gain'.

Map the 'drone' macro: dry/wet over 0–99; utility on/off+gain so 100–110 is silent; freeze ('infinite') and overdub ('add') switch on at ≥110; LFO on/off, rate (fast at 110 → ~0.1 Hz at max), jitter and wave shape (≈75%→20%) across 110–127; auto-filter on and its LFO time also on this range.
LFO device targets with depths: mid-EQ frequency 30, mid gain −25, low EQ 15, high EQ −20, width 15.
Auto filter: frequency ~1500 Hz, resonance 10%, MS-type model, drive 5%, clip on; its own LFO in time mode at 10% amount, deliberately not synced to the rack LFO.
Play: below 100 use as a normal reverb; above 110 play a note or two and let them overdub into the frozen space; adjust mid/high/low EQ in real time if boomy or trebly.
Randomize the rack (exclude EQ, pre-delay and drone macros) to audition reverb spaces; save good results as rack variations and re-save the rack preset.

variants.name: Stereo delay motion: ping-pong, dual-parallel, two-tap, cross-feedback
variants.goal: Build musical stereo delay motion for synths/pads: tempo-synced ping-pong (feedback ~40–50%, wet ~15–25%, repeats band-limited ~100 Hz–3 kHz, optional saturation, even or offset L/R), dual-parallel (independent L/R subdivisions such as dotted-eighth vs quarter, self-feedback then cross-feedback, optional modulation/diffusion for reverb-like density), two-tap tape-head (long tap feeds short; short has no self/cross feedback), ping-pong recognized as a 2:1 two-tap, LFO panning delay and feedback-phase invert; prefer send routing and automate for evolving motion.
steps: Pick the delay topology for the job: ping-pong bounce (discreet L↔R, steps 2–5), dual-parallel with optional cross-feedback (dense poly-rhythmic space, steps 6–9), two-tap tape-head style (cleaner bounce, steps 10–11), or LFO panning delay (step 12). Then route and animate it (steps 13–14).
Ping-pong: Enable ping-pong / stereo bounce delay. Set delay time to a musical subdivision (quarter or eighth) so repeats lock to groove.
Ping-pong: Set feedback ~40–50% so repeats fade without clutter; wet/dry ~15–25% as a starting mix.
Ping-pong: Filter the delayed signal: cut lows below ~100 Hz and highs above ~3 kHz to avoid mud/harshness. Optionally add tiny saturation/distortion on wet for warmth.
Ping-pong: Maximize stereo width of the bounce when desired; link L/R times for even bounce, or slightly offset L vs R times for a more complex image.

Start dual-parallel: set different tempo subdivisions per channel (e.g. dotted-eighth left, quarter right) so the shorter and longer echoes interact as a delay poly-rhythm (classic 3-against-4 feel with those two).
Set self-feedback per channel (example starting points from transcript: ~45% left into left, ~30% right into right) with no cross-feedback yet; hear space/energy without stacked interaction.
Add cross-feedback (right→left, then optionally left→right with complementary amounts) to stack interacting delays and fill the stereo field toward a faux-reverb density.
Optional lush pad/ambient path: raise delay modulation depth (~20% in source demo) and diffusion (~50%) so dual-delay + cross-feedback reads more like reverb-space.

Build two-tap (multi-head tape style): keep long + short times, but only the longer delay self-feeds and also feeds the shorter delay; give the shorter delay zero self-feedback and zero cross-feedback so taps never line up like dual-parallel — cleaner stereo around a center dry signal.

Recognize ping-pong as a two-tap with ~2:1 time ratio (e.g. 400 ms / 800 ms) and the same long→short + long self-feedback topology; prefer dedicated ping-pong mode when available. Contrast with dual-parallel at 2:1 (short and long land together, soft-panned long tap).

Optional: panning delay uses an LFO to move repeats (syncable for ping-pong-like motion or offset rates). Feedback-phase invert (negative feedback phase) flips polarity each regeneration to enhance spatial width on cross-feedback designs. Keep mix lower in practice; use ducking/EQ on wet for dense sources.
Prefer send routing so you can EQ/compress the wet alone before blend; if insert, mind wet/dry carefully.

Automate or modulate feedback, delay time, or filter cutoff across sections; optional subtle chorus/flanger on delayed signal only. Use on synths (also vocals/guitars/perc) especially in sparse/breakdown sections.

variants.name: EQ chorus dual-delay multi-algo reverb FX chain
variants.goal: Finish a cinematic patch with the Traveler-style FX order: 3-band EQ → multi-type chorus → dual/ping-pong modulated delay → room/hall/space reverb (long space tails).
steps: Insert 3-band EQ first: sculpt low end, mid presence, and highs so the synth sits in a mix before time FX.
Add chorus: choose type 1, type 2, or combined. Keep wet modest for cinematic width without seasick detune.
Dual or ping-pong stereo modulated delay: independent L/R times, feedback, stereo spread, feedback filters, and classic delay modulation.
Reverb: pick room, hall, or space algorithm (space can reach very long tails). Set size/decay/predelay manually with original settings.
Map portable names: KeyTIME-like = tempo-synced modulated delay motion; KeySPACE-like = multi-algo cinematic reverb. Keep FX after synth engine; watch limiter on main out.

variants.name: Filtered feedback-delay resonator: bipolar feedback, swappable loop filter type, dry mute, insert on existing sounds
variants.goal: Turn a single filtered feedback delay into a playable 'renegade' Karplus-Strong voice and a resonator insert: impulse (noise burst or fast sine sweep, no loop) into a ~1–24 ms delay with feedback limited to ±99% (negative = hollow/odd-harmonic, positive = brighter), macro the in-loop filter type (LP/HP/BP/notch, with resonance on BP/notch) and cutoff as timbre controls, mute the dry click, map keys inversely onto delay time (long = low), then reuse the same delay as a metallic-body resonator on basses/pads — the delta beyond our key-tracked KS pluck skill is bipolar feedback polarity, loop-filter-type morphing, dry-mute and the resonator-insert use.
steps: Prepare a full-frequency impulse: a short white-noise burst or a fast sine sweep from very high to low frequency. Set it to one-shot (no loop) so it is only a click.
Insert a delay with feedback and an in-loop filter. Start around 24 ms delay, feedback 50%, effect amount full, filter low-pass fully open.

Make performance macros: (1) L+R feedback with range −99…+99 (centre = almost no repeats; negative = hollow square-like character; positive = saw-like), (2) delay time L+R capped at ~24 ms as 'pitch', (3) filter cutoff.
For keyboard pitch: map key tracking onto delay time inversely — lowest key → ~24 ms (slow cycle = low pitch), highest key → ~1 ms.
Add a macro for filter type (LP/HP/BP/notch) and automate/record it. With bandpass or notch, raise resonance somewhat — they sound better slightly resonant.
Mute the dry signal so the impulse click disappears and only the resonance remains; optionally add drive in the loop (can scream) and a following delay.
Try different impulse sources (sine, saw, more or less pitched) — the impulse strongly changes the timbre.
Resonator insert: put the same delay (wrapped in a macro rack) on an existing bass or pad; tune delay/filter to taste (check filter isn't left on high-pass), keep it subtle or brighter/distorted.
Resample interesting results for further processing.
